title: Reasoning under uncertainty in humans and language models
claim: Comparing agents on an active reasoning task, then fitting interpretable latent parameters, places all agents in one shared cognitive space.
layout: 4 panels A–D, left-to-right, task to behavior to model to space
description: A wide four-panel strip labeled A–D, read left to right: Task, Behavior, Mechanisms, Cognitive Space. Panel A shows stacked cards for Rounds 1, 2 and N. Each card has buttons A–D, some red or green, and the last card has a dark inference grid of '?' buttons. Panel B shows horizontal bars for performance, sampling-inference and invalid choices. The bars are colored purple, crimson, orange and peach for the models, with gray marking reasoning versus no-reasoning. Panel C shows a cluster of colored people icons, for LLMs, humans and the optimal agent, with an arrow to a hub-and-spoke model. The spokes are Memory β, Strategy κ, Occlusion Awareness θ and Choice Biases ω, γ. Panel D shows a cross-shaped plot with axes from Stubborn to Forgetful and from Random to Rational. Colored dots sit on the plot, and gray arrows show the effect of reasoning.
caption: From task performance to latent cognitive variables. A: Task. An active probabilistic reasoning task in which agents sequentially sample from up to four buttons (A–D), each revealing a binary outcome (RED/GREEN). One button is biased toward RED, while the others are unbiased. During T sampling rounds, agents sample evidence among the buttons available. During inference round, agents indicate which button they believe is biased. An equivalent text-based version is used for LLMs (App. B.1). B: Behavior. Comparison of human and LLM behavior by overall performance, sampling/inference quality, and invalid choices. These metrics reveal a broad spectrum of performance, with extended reasoning improving overall success via enhanced inference, while gains in sampling remain limited. C: Mechanisms. Behavioral model that captures deviations from optimal Bayesian inference using interpretable parameters: Memory (β), Strategy (m, κf), Choice Bias (ω, γ), and Occlusion Awareness (θs, θf). D: Cognitive space. These parameters define a shared low-dimensional space for humans and LLMs. Reasoning shifts LLMs toward human-like inference strategies, and tightens the gap in sampling strategies.
abstract: Do language models make decisions under uncertainty like humans do? And if so, what role does extended reasoning play in the underlying decision process? We answer this question by introducing an active probabilistic reasoning task that cleanly separates sampling (actively acquiring evidence) from inference (integrating evidence towards a decision). Benchmarking humans and a broad set of contemporary LLMs against an optimal reference policy reveals a consistent pattern: extended reasoning is the key determinant of strong performance, driving large gains in inference, while yielding only modest improvements in active sampling. To explain these differences, we fit a behavioral model that captures systematic deviations from optimal Bayesian behavior through interpretable parameter families, placing humans and models in a shared low-dimensional cognitive space. The resulting fits show how reasoning shifts models toward human-like regimes of evidence accumulation and belief-to-choice mapping, and yield testable predictions about the latent dynamics that might drive each decision. Probing residual-stream activations of an open-weight reasoning model, we find that the geometry of internal representations tracks these predicted dynamics, linking behavior to representational correlates of the fitted latent dynamics.
